title: When Locusts Swarm
passage:
Most of the time, the desert locust is a shy, solitary grasshopper that lives quietly in the dry regions of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and south-west Asia. It is usually green or brown, and it avoids other locusts. However, under certain conditions, this harmless insect can transform into one of the most destructive pests in the world.

The change begins after unusually heavy rain. Plants grow quickly, and female locusts lay large numbers of eggs in the damp sand. When the vegetation later dries up, the young locusts are forced to crowd together on the remaining patches of green. Constant contact with one another causes surprising changes in their bodies and behaviour. They become brightly coloured, they start moving in groups, and eventually the adults form enormous flying swarms.

A single swarm can contain tens of millions of locusts and can travel more than one hundred kilometres in a day with the help of the wind. Each locust eats roughly its own weight in fresh food daily, so a large swarm can destroy entire fields of crops within hours. For farmers, this can mean losing a whole season's harvest.

To prevent such disasters, countries including Saudi Arabia work with international organisations to monitor rainfall and vegetation in the desert. When teams discover young locusts gathering, they treat the area quickly, before the insects are able to fly.

questions.stem: The word "locusts" is plural. Which word from the passage is SINGULAR?
options: swarm
insects
eggs
plants
questions.why: "Swarm" names one group; the other words end in -s and mean more than one.

questions.stem: Locusts can become "destructive pests." Which sentence uses the word "destructive" correctly?
options: Her destructive smile made everyone feel welcome.
We ate a destructive lunch of rice and fish.
The destructive storm knocked down many trees.
The baby slept in a soft and destructive bed.
questions.why: "Destructive" means causing great damage; a storm that knocks down trees is destructive.

questions.stem: Why are young locusts forced to crowd together?
options: Heavy rain floods the sand where they were born.
The plants dry up, leaving only small green patches.
Strong winds blow them into one small corner.
Farmers trap them together in their fields.
questions.why: "When the vegetation later dries up, the young locusts are forced to crowd together on the remaining patches of green."

questions.stem: Which event happens FIRST in the change from a solitary locust to a swarm?
options: Unusually heavy rain falls in the desert.
The adults form enormous flying swarms.
The young locusts become brightly coloured.
The vegetation dries up in the hot sun.
questions.why: The passage says "the change begins after unusually heavy rain."

questions.stem: How is a solitary locust DIFFERENT from a swarming locust?
options: It eats much more food and flies much farther.
It is green or brown and stays away from others.
It is brightly coloured and travels in groups.
It lives only in fields where farmers grow crops.
questions.why: Solitary locusts are "green or brown" and avoid other locusts; swarming locusts are brightly coloured and move in groups.

questions.stem: The writer says "this harmless insect can transform into one of the most destructive pests in the world." What is the effect of contrasting "harmless" and "destructive"?
options: It shows that the writer is unsure what locusts are.
It suggests that locusts are never really dangerous.
It stresses how surprising and serious the change is.
It proves that all grasshoppers become pests one day.
questions.why: Placing opposite words together emphasises the dramatic change and grabs the reader's attention.

questions.stem: Which opinion is BEST supported by the passage?
options: Locust swarms are impossible to stop once rain has fallen.
Only farmers need to worry about desert locusts.
Heavy rain in the desert is always good news for farmers.
Finding young locusts early is the best way to protect crops.
questions.why: The passage explains that teams treat young locusts "before the insects are able to fly," preventing disasters.

questions.stem: Which information in the passage is the LEAST clear or complete?
options: How far a swarm can travel in a single day
How the teams treat an area where locusts gather
Where female locusts lay their eggs
What colour a solitary locust usually is
questions.why: The passage says teams "treat the area quickly" but does not explain what this treatment is.

questions.stem: Which of the following events could REALLY happen?
options: A locust swarm eats a whole city's buildings.
A single locust carries a farmer across the sea.
Locust numbers rise in a desert after heavy rain.
Locusts lay their eggs in the clouds above the desert.
questions.why: Heavy rain helps plants grow and locusts breed, so their numbers can rise; the others are impossible.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is the BEST way to stop a swarm from destroying crops?
options: Wait until the swarm leaves on its own.
Plant more crops after the swarm arrives.
Stop all rain from falling in the desert.
Treat young locusts before they can fly.
questions.why: Monitoring teams treat areas where young locusts gather "before the insects are able to fly."
